claims.text: The initial alloy is a single-phase Ti–Ni high-entropy alloy.
Titanium and nickel are primary constituents of the initial alloy.
The initial alloy contains no secondary carbide phases.
A trace carbon addition during melting and casting will promote in-situ TiC formation in the Ti–Ni alloy.
The carbon-induced TiC precipitates will be nanoscale and dispersed throughout the Ti–Ni HEA matrix.
Carbide particles can impede dislocation motion through particle-related strengthening mechanisms.
TiC particles will impede grain-boundary sliding in the Ti–Ni HEA at elevated temperature.
Carbon-induced TiC precipitation will increase the alloy's elevated-temperature strength and hardness.
TiC particles will act as diffusion barriers that inhibit rapid high-temperature oxidation.
The carbon-added alloy will have better oxidation resistance than the carbon-free baseline.
The proposed strengthening and oxidation effects are applicable around 800 °C and under aggressive oxidizing conditions.
Excess carbon may produce coarse precipitates and invalidate the proposed benefit.
Related HEA systems have exhibited in-situ carbide-particle strengthening.
The precipitation behavior, high-temperature stability, and mechanical contribution of nanoscale TiC in a Ti–Ni-dominant HEA remain unvalidated.

contradictions.description: The mediator requires a secondary TiC precipitate phase, while the boundary says the processed alloy is to maintain a single-phase solid-solution structure. These are incompatible if 'single-phase' describes the whole post-intervention microstructure rather than only the matrix.
